analysis.one_liner: Forces freight railroads to compete for captive customers and gives shippers a way to challenge high rates.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 12 bipartisan cosponsors and got a Senate subcommittee hearing, but the Senate Commerce Committee never voted on it, and it died when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A handful of giant freight railroads control most of the country's rail lines, and many farmers, timber producers, utilities, and factories can ship only on one of them, which lets the railroad charge rates far above its costs. This bill would direct the regulator (the Surface Transportation Board) to foster real competition: it would require railroads to let competitors switch cars on their tracks where practical, bar line sales that cut off other railroads' access, create an independent Rail Customer Advocate, publish customer complaints, give shippers a faster and cheaper process to challenge rates, and require arbitration of certain disputes. It never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Captive rail customers — grain farmers, timber and paper producers, coal-dependent utilities, and manufacturers served by only one railroad — plus consumers who ultimately pay for freight in food, electricity, and goods prices. Small shippers of agricultural and forestry commodities get special attention in the bill.

how_it_helps.text: Requires railroads to provide a rate and service between any two points on their system on a shipper's request, ending refusals to quote rates to captive customers [S3].

Makes reciprocal switching — letting a competing railroad serve a customer's facility — mandatory where the regulator finds it practical and in the public interest, and the regulator cannot demand proof of anticompetitive conduct first [S2][S3].

Lets state governors petition to have a region served by a single Class I railroad declared an 'area of inadequate rail competition' when shippers pay rates above 180% of variable costs, and orders remedies like switching and trackage rights within 60 days [S3].
Creates an Office of Rail Customer Advocacy in the Transportation Department to take complaints, intervene in regulator proceedings, and access railroad data [S2][S3].

Gives shippers facing a railroad with 'market dominance' a right to a cost-effective process for rate challenges based on the railroad's actual costs, with the railroad required to prove its rate is reasonable once market dominance is shown, and caps filing fees at what district courts charge [S3].
Requires arbitration of certain agricultural and timber freight disputes at either party's election, with decisions appealable only under a clear-error standard [S2][S3].
Requires the regulator to investigate rail-carrier violations on its own initiative and to investigate any complaint it receives, rather than only on complaint [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The large Class I freight railroads, whose pricing power over captive customers would be curtailed and who would have to share terminal access and answer rate challenges. Any reduction in the above-cost margins railroads earn on captive traffic could, over time, reduce the revenue they have available for infrastructure investment.

drawbacks.text: Rail lines have enormous fixed costs, and rates above variable cost are how railroads recover them; capping rates near the 180% variable-cost threshold could shrink funds available for maintaining and expanding track, an objection the industry and some economists have long raised about cost-based rate regulation (general policy knowledge; the bill sets that 180% threshold at [S3]).

Mandated reciprocal switching and arbitration add regulatory proceedings and compliance costs, and the bill's complaint-publication requirement would put service problems in public view, which railroads argued would air operational disputes without context (mechanism at [S2][S3]).

The bill relies on the regulator to act within tight deadlines on complex rate cases; if the Surface Transportation Board lacks the capacity to meet them, shippers could still be left with slow, expensive relief (deadlines at [S3]).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's protections are aimed at a genuine monopoly problem — shippers with no alternative railroad paying rates the bill itself treats as excessive above 180% of variable cost — and its remedies (switching, rate challenges, arbitration, an advocate) are targeted rather than a full re-regulation of rates. The main real cost is that railroads' above-cost revenue funds their network investment, so squeezing captive-traffic margins could eventually affect service and infrastructure spending. On balance it shifts bargaining power from a concentrated industry to its captive customers at a moderate, uncertain cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, got a subcommittee hearing in October 2007, and then sat there with no committee vote or floor action until the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rockefeller introduced the bill on March 21, 2007, joined at introduction by a bipartisan group of senators from farm, timber, and coal states [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
The Commerce Committee's Surface Transportation subcommittee held a hearing on the bill on October 23, 2007 [S5].
After the hearing, the committee took no further action — no markup, no vote, no Senate floor consideration — and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Class I freight railroads kept the status quo: no mandatory switching, no rate-challenge overhaul, and no independent customer advocate. Their customers, and the consumers behind them, kept paying the prevailing freight rates.

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.role: Senate sponsor, chairing influence on railroad issues as a senator from a coal-hauling state
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks for it.

for.name: 12 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors — 4 of 49 Senate Republicans and 8 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, including Sens. Craig, Vitter, and Crapo (R) and Dorgan, Klobuchar, Tester, Landrieu, Baucus, and Cantwell (D).

for.name: Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Surface Transportation and Merchant Marine Infrastructure, Safety, and Security
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on October 23, 2007.

against.name: Sen. Daniel Inouye
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: His committee referred the bill to a subcommittee and held a hearing, but never brought it to a committee vote or the Senate floor.

against.name: Class I freight railroads
against.role: The major national freight railroads (Union Pacific, BNSF, CSX, Norfolk Southern and peers)
against.what_they_did: Opposed reciprocal-switching mandates and rate regulation through lobbying; the industry has consistently fought bills of this kind, and none advanced while they opposed it.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 4 Republicans and 8 Democrats among 12 cosponsors — and the record shows no recorded vote, so party lines on the substance never got tested.

industries.industry: Class I freight railroads (Union Pacific, BNSF, CSX, Norfolk Southern and peers)
industries.note: These carriers hold near-monopoly positions over many shippers and would lose pricing freedom above cost, face mandatory reciprocal switching, and answer to a customer advocate and faster rate challenges. Their gain from captive customers is ordinary people's cost in food, electricity, and goods prices.

industries.industry: Agricultural and forestry shippers (grain, timber, paper, fertilizer)
industries.note: The bill gives these shippers mandatory arbitration, special study of their rate problems, and a workable process to challenge rates they currently cannot contest. Savings would flow partly to farmers and producers and partly to consumers through lower prices.

industries.industry: Short-line railroads (Class II and III carriers)
industries.note: The bill bars line transfers from Class I carriers that restrict short lines' ability to interchange traffic or that raise their interchange rates, and lets them or affected shippers ask the regulator to strike such restrictions. This keeps small regional railroads connected to the national network, which supports local service and jobs.
